BRIEF_STORY.p: On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and two days later Britain and France declared war. The Polish army fought hard, but it was outnumbered, attacked from three sides and, from 17 September, stabbed in the back by the Soviet Union under the secret terms of the Nazi–Soviet Pact. Warsaw surrendered on 28 September and the last Polish forces on 6 October. The country was divided between two dictatorships. The Germans set out to destroy the Polish elite and to crowd Poland's Jews into ghettos; in the east, the Soviets deported hundreds of thousands and in 1940 shot some 22,000 Polish prisoners at Katyn and other sites.

After a winter of 'Phoney War', Germany seized Denmark and Norway in April 1940. On 10 May it attacked the Netherlands, Belgium and France. The British and French moved their best armies into Belgium, but the main German blow came through the Ardennes: on 13 May the panzers crossed the Meuse at Sedan and in a week reached the Channel, trapping the northern armies. Some 338,000 men were evacuated from Dunkirk, but France was beaten. It signed an armistice at Compiègne on 22 June, and the Vichy regime under Pétain collaborated with the occupier.

Churchill refused to negotiate. In the summer of 1940 the Luftwaffe tried to win control of the air over southern England as a prelude to invasion and failed against the RAF's radar-directed fighters; on 17 September Hitler postponed the invasion. The Blitz on British cities went on until May 1941. In the Atlantic the U-boats attacked the convoys that kept Britain alive, while Italy's entry into the war opened fronts in North Africa and the Mediterranean. Germany rescued its ally by conquering Yugoslavia and Greece in April 1941 and Crete in May, and sent Rommel to Libya.

On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with more than three million men. The Red Army lost millions killed and captured in vast encirclements, and by the autumn the Germans were outside Leningrad and Moscow. Behind them the Einsatzgruppen shot Jewish communities by the tens of thousands, as at Babi Yar in September. But the Soviet state did not collapse. Its factories were moved east, its reserves were thrown in, and on 5 December Zhukov counter-attacked before Moscow. Two days later Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and on 11 December Hitler declared war on the United States.

At Wannsee in January 1942 senior officials coordinated the deportation and murder of all Europe's Jews. Death camps were built in occupied Poland — Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibór and Treblinka, then Auschwitz-Birkenau and Majdanek — and trains came to them from France, the Netherlands, Greece, Italy, Hungary and everywhere German power reached. In 1942 alone some 2.7 million Jews were killed. By 1945 about six million had been murdered, along with Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, disabled people and others. In the Warsaw ghetto in 1943, and at Treblinka and Sobibór, Jews rose against their killers.

In 1942 Germany struck again in the East, towards the Caucasus oilfields and the Volga. At Stalingrad the Sixth Army was drawn into a street battle, and in November the Red Army encircled it; Paulus surrendered at the start of February 1943. In North Africa the British won at El Alamein in November 1942 and Anglo-American forces landed in Morocco and Algeria; the Axis armies in Tunisia surrendered in May 1943. That same month the escorts beat the U-boats in the Atlantic. In July Germany's last great offensive in the East, at Kursk, failed within a week.

From mid-1943 Germany was on the defensive everywhere. The Allies landed in Sicily in July and in Italy in September; Mussolini fell and Italy changed sides, but the Germans held most of the peninsula and fought the Allies to a standstill at Monte Cassino until May 1944. The British and American bomber offensive burned Hamburg in July 1943 and in early 1944 destroyed the Luftwaffe's fighter force. In the East the Red Army advanced across Ukraine and in January 1944 ended the siege of Leningrad. Across occupied Europe resistance grew, and so did German reprisals.

On 6 June 1944 the Western Allies landed in Normandy. For ten weeks they fought a bitter battle in the hedgerows and around Caen, until the Americans broke out in late July and two German armies were nearly trapped in the Falaise pocket. Paris was freed on 25 August. In the East, Operation Bagration destroyed Army Group Centre in Belarus from 22 June, and the Red Army reached the Vistula. On 20 July Stauffenberg's bomb failed to kill Hitler. On 1 August the Polish Home Army rose in Warsaw; the Soviets halted across the river, and after 63 days the Rising was crushed.

The Allied pursuit ran out of fuel at the German frontier. Market Garden, the airborne gamble to cross the Rhine at Arnhem in September, failed. Through the autumn the Americans fought slow, costly battles at Aachen and in the Hürtgen Forest. In the Balkans, Romania and Bulgaria changed sides and the Germans left Greece. On 16 December Hitler threw his last reserves into the Ardennes. The Battle of the Bulge took the Americans by surprise, but Bastogne held, and by January the German army had lost the strength it could no longer replace.

In January 1945 the Red Army swept from the Vistula to the Oder, freeing Auschwitz on 27 January. In the west the Allies cleared the Rhineland, crossed the Rhine at Remagen on 7 March and in strength on 23–24 March, and encircled the Ruhr. As they advanced, they found the camps — Buchenwald, Belsen, Dachau — and the world saw what had been done. On 16 April the Soviets attacked towards Berlin; on 25 April Americans and Soviets met on the Elbe. Hitler killed himself on 30 April. Germany surrendered unconditionally at Reims on 7 May and at Karlshorst late on 8 May.

WHY: No one place explains the Second World War in Europe. Westerplatte and Sedan show how fast Germany won in 1939–40; Uxbridge, Bletchley and the Western Approaches bunker show how Britain held on. The cemeteries of Normandy and the memorials of Stalingrad and Prokhorovka show where the war was decided and at what cost. The camps — Treblinka, Auschwitz, Dachau, Belsen — and villages such as Lidice and Oradour show what the war was for in Nazi eyes, and what victory stopped. Seen together, from Gdańsk to Karlshorst, the places add up to one war: a war of armies, industry and codes, and of genocide.
CAVEATS: The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people, soldiers and civilians, according to the figure published in 1990 from demographic calculations; Stalin had admitted 7 million, Khrushchev 20 million. For military deaths, the Russian General Staff study led by G. F. Krivosheev gives about 8.7 million, including prisoners who died in captivity. Some Russian and Western researchers argue that this is too low and that military dead may have exceeded 11 million. Civilian deaths are harder still to count, because the borders of 1941 and the population of the occupied lands are themselves uncertain.

On 24 May 1940 Hitler confirmed a halt of the panzers short of Dunkirk, which gave the Allies time to organise the perimeter and the evacuation. Why is still argued. The halt was proposed by Rundstedt, commanding Army Group A, to rest and repair his tanks for the battle still to come in the south and to avoid the canals and marshes round Dunkirk; Göring promised that the Luftwaffe could finish the job. The idea that Hitler let the British go to make peace easier comes mainly from later claims and is doubted by most historians.

Soviet histories described Prokhorovka on 12 July 1943 as the greatest tank battle in history, with some 1,500 tanks and a German armoured force smashed. Research in German and Soviet archives since the 1990s — by Karl-Heinz Frieser, Valeriy Zamulin, David Glantz and others — shows roughly 600 Soviet tanks and self-propelled guns against fewer than 300 German. The Soviets lost around 300–400 tanks that day; German permanent losses were small, perhaps only a handful, though many more were damaged. The Soviet attack nevertheless stopped the SS Panzer Corps, and the offensive was called off.

For decades, figures of 135,000, 200,000 or even more were quoted for the dead of the February 1945 raids on Dresden. They began with Nazi propaganda, which added a nought to a police report, and were spread after the war, notably by David Irving on the basis of a forged document. A historians' commission set up by the city reported in 2010 that between 18,000 and 25,000 people died. The moral argument over the raid — military necessity or terror bombing — continues separately from the numbers.

When Germany announced the discovery of the Katyn graves in April 1943, the Soviet Union blamed the Germans, broke off relations with the Polish government in London when it asked for a Red Cross inquiry, and in 1944 produced its own commission report. The Soviets even raised Katyn at the Nuremberg trials, where the charge was quietly dropped. Western governments, needing Stalin, said little. Only in 1990 did the Soviet Union admit that the NKVD had carried out the killings; some Russian investigation files remain closed, and the full list of victims from Belarus has never been published.
Why did the Red Army stop at Warsaw?

When the Home Army rose in August 1944, the Red Army stood a few kilometres from Warsaw and then halted. One view stresses military reasons: the Soviet armies were exhausted after advancing hundreds of kilometres in Bagration, and German panzer divisions had just defeated their spearhead north-east of the city. The other stresses Stalin's politics: he wanted no independent Polish authority in the capital, and for weeks refused Allied supply aircraft the use of Soviet airfields. Most historians accept that both played a part; they disagree on the balance.

Montgomery called Market Garden '90 per cent successful'; others see it as an avoidable failure. Blame has been laid on the plan's single road, on intelligence warnings about SS panzer units near Arnhem that were discounted, on drop zones 10–13 km from the bridge, on radios that did not work, on the delay at Nijmegen and on the slow advance of XXX Corps. Major-General Sosabowski of the Polish Parachute Brigade, who had warned against the plan, was removed from command afterwards — a decision widely seen today as unjust.

Early post-war figures for individual camps were often far too high: a Soviet commission put the dead of Auschwitz at 4 million, which stood on the memorial until 1990, and Majdanek's at 1.5 million. Research in the camp records, transport lists and population data has since produced lower, better-founded figures — about 1.1 million for Auschwitz (Franciszek Piper), about 78,000 for Majdanek (Tomasz Kranz). Treblinka estimates range from about 800,000 to 925,000. These revisions do not change the total of about six million Jews murdered, which rests on separate population studies.

Some 2,900 aircrew of Fighter Command took part in the Battle of Britain, and about 544 were killed. They were not only British: about one in five came from elsewhere, including Poles, Czechs, New Zealanders, Canadians and others, and the Polish No. 303 Squadron had the best record of any. Nor were they hopelessly outnumbered in fighters. Their success owed much to radar and the control system, to Hurricanes as much as Spitfires, and to German errors. Some historians argue that the Royal Navy, rather than Fighter Command alone, was the real barrier to invasion.

paras.p: The Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919, took territory from Germany in the east and west, limited its army to 100,000 men with no tanks or aircraft, demilitarised the Rhineland and made it pay reparations. Most Germans regarded the treaty as a dictated peace, and the claim that the army had been 'stabbed in the back' at home in 1918 poisoned politics. Poland was reborn, with a corridor to the sea that cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany; Danzig became a Free City under the League of Nations.

The new democracies of central Europe survived the 1920s, but the world economic crisis after 1929 broke the Weimar Republic. By early 1932 about six million Germans were out of work. Voters turned to the extremes, and the Nazi Party became the largest in the Reichstag that July. Elsewhere, too, democracy was in retreat: Italy had been Fascist since 1922, and by the late 1930s most states between the Baltic and the Aegean were run by dictators or authoritarian governments.

Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Within months the Reichstag fire was used to suspend civil rights, the Enabling Act let him rule by decree, other parties were banned and the first concentration camp opened at Dachau. Jews were driven out of public life and, by the Nuremberg Laws of 1935, stripped of citizenship.

Germany left the League of Nations in October 1933, announced conscription and an air force in March 1935 and sent troops into the demilitarised Rhineland on 7 March 1936. Britain and France protested and did nothing. In the Spanish Civil War, from July 1936, the Luftwaffe's Condor Legion gained combat experience, bombing Guernica in April 1937, while Mussolini's Italy, after conquering Ethiopia, drew closer to Hitler in the Rome–Berlin Axis.

Hitler's aims went far beyond revising Versailles. He wanted 'living space' (Lebensraum) in the East, to be won by war against the Soviet Union and settled by Germans at the expense of the Slav peoples, and he saw the Jews as the enemy behind both Bolshevism and the Western democracies.

In March 1938 German troops marched into Austria, and the Anschluss made it part of the Reich. Hitler next demanded the Sudetenland, the German-speaking border regions of Czechoslovakia, a democracy allied to France with strong frontier fortifications.

Britain's Prime Minister, Neville Chamberlain, believed a general war could be avoided by meeting Germany's 'reasonable' grievances, and Britain and France were not ready to fight. At Munich on 29–30 September 1938 Britain, France and Italy agreed that Germany should take the Sudetenland; the Czechoslovaks were not even at the table. Chamberlain returned promising 'peace for our time'. Historians still argue whether appeasement was cowardice or a realistic way of buying time to rearm; it certainly bought time for Germany as well.

On the night of 9–10 November 1938, in the Kristallnacht pogrom, synagogues and Jewish shops were destroyed across Germany. On 15 March 1939 Hitler occupied what remained of the Czech lands. This was no German grievance, and British opinion turned. On 31 March Britain and France guaranteed Poland's independence. Hitler now demanded Danzig and a route across the Polish corridor.

Britain and France held half-hearted talks with the Soviet Union in the summer of 1939; Poland would not allow Soviet troops onto its soil. Stalin, distrustful of the West after Munich, took the better offer. On 23 August 1939 the German and Soviet foreign ministers, Ribbentrop and Molotov, signed a non-aggression pact in Moscow. A secret protocol divided eastern Europe into spheres: western Poland and Lithuania for Germany (Lithuania was soon traded), eastern Poland, the Baltic states, Finland and Bessarabia for the Soviet Union.

Free of the danger of a war on two fronts, Hitler attacked Poland on 1 September 1939, after the SS staged a fake Polish attack on the radio station at Gleiwitz. Britain, which had signed an alliance with Poland on 25 August, and France declared war on 3 September. The Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September and supplied Germany with oil, grain and raw materials until June 1941.

Almost every army used the same ladder: sections or squads of about ten men, platoons of about thirty, companies of about 120, battalions of 600–900, regiments or brigades of three battalions, and divisions of 10,000–18,000 men with their own artillery, engineers and supply. Two to five divisions made a corps, several corps an army, and several armies an army group — called a Front in the Red Army.

The German army of 1939–40 was mostly infantry that marched on foot with horse-drawn supply; its edge came from a small number of panzer divisions, close air support and well-trained junior leaders encouraged to use initiative. It grew to well over 200 divisions, many of them worn down to a fraction of their strength by 1944. The Waffen-SS expanded alongside it, and from 1944 the Volksgrenadier divisions and the Volkssturm militia filled the gaps with older men and boys.

Britain sent a small, fully motorised Expeditionary Force to France in 1939–40. It grew into a citizen army that fought alongside contingents from Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India — whose army became the largest volunteer force in history — and was strongest in artillery. Infantry divisions of three brigades were backed by armoured divisions and independent tank brigades.

France mobilised about five million men behind the Maginot Line in 1939. Its army had good tanks but spread many of them among infantry units, relied on slow communications and was organised for a methodical war like 1918. After 1942 the Free French and the army of North Africa, re-equipped by the Americans, fought in Tunisia, Italy and France.

The US Army grew from fewer than 200,000 men in 1939 to more than eight million in 1945, including the Army Air Forces, and fielded 89 divisions. Its divisions were fully motorised, supplied on a lavish scale and supported by plentiful artillery with very good fire control.

The Red Army was purged of much of its senior command in 1937–38 and was caught reorganising in 1941. It lost millions of men that year but rebuilt itself: rifle divisions were smaller than western ones, while tank and mechanised corps and massed artillery were concentrated for breakthroughs. By 1944 it was a skilled, hard-hitting force, though still careless of casualties, and moved by American-built lorries.

Poland mobilised about a million men in 1939, with infantry divisions and cavalry brigades but few tanks or modern aircraft. After its defeat, Poles fought on in the west — in France in 1940, in the Battle of Britain, at Tobruk, Monte Cassino, Falaise and Arnhem — while the Home Army fought underground at home and a Soviet-sponsored Polish army fought its way from the east to Berlin.

The murder of Europe's Jews cannot be told apart from the war. Conquest brought millions of Jews under German control: about 3.3 million in Poland, millions more in the occupied Soviet Union. Persecution became mass murder with the invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, when the Einsatzgruppen began shooting whole communities, and systematic deportation to death camps followed from 1942. About six million Jews were murdered, along with Roma, people with disabilities, Soviet prisoners of war and others.

Many of the places in this guide — Wannsee, Treblinka, Auschwitz, Majdanek, Babi Yar, Dachau, Belsen and the Anne Frank House — belong to this story. They are places of memory and of mourning, and some are graves. Dress and behave accordingly, follow the memorials' rules on photography, and allow time: these are not sites to hurry through.
